label: Smooth Maps
notes: This chapter, printed pages 32 through 49, teaches one reflex: never differentiate on the abstract set itself, translate into a chart and run ordinary calculus there. We meet smooth functions, smooth maps, diffeomorphisms, and the analytic engine of bump functions and partitions of unity that turns local data into global objects.

label: Smooth Functions in Charts
notes: A scalar function is smooth when its coordinate representation, the composite with an inverse chart, is ordinary smooth on a Euclidean open set. Stress that the manifold has no intrinsic notion of partial derivative; the chart supplies it. The example, x squared plus y squared becoming r squared in polar coordinates, shows the test in action.

label: Independence of Charts
notes: Walk students through why the chart choice does not matter: any two overlapping charts differ by a smooth transition map, so composing with it preserves ordinary smoothness. This is the well-definedness argument that justifies the whole definition. Without smooth transitions on the atlas, the word smooth would have no meaning on the manifold.

label: Smooth Maps Between Manifolds
notes: Now there are two translations, one on the source and one on the target. The coordinate representation psi after F after phi inverse must be ordinary smooth. Emphasize the target-chart landing condition: the image of the small neighborhood must sit inside the target chart domain. That requirement is exactly what forces smooth maps to be continuous.

label: Coordinate Representation Visual
notes: Spend time on this diagram; it is the mental model for the entire course. Two manifolds sit on top, two Euclidean patches below, and the downstairs arrow is the only thing we ever compute with. The map upstairs is abstract; the hat-F downstairs is concrete calculus. Every later smoothness proof reduces to drawing this square.

label: The Circle Example
notes: The exponential parametrization t maps to e to the two pi i t is the cleanest coordinate-square example. Around any point avoiding a chart cut, an angle chart unwraps a short arc and the coordinate expression is simply linear in t, hence smooth. Use it to show that smoothness is checked locally, point by point, never all at once.

label: Failure Modes
notes: Two honest warnings. A step function looks locally constant on each side of its jump, yet it is not continuous, so it is not smooth; the target-chart condition rules it out. And absolute value, smooth on each closed half-line, develops a cusp where the pieces meet. Locality is real, but continuity and overlap agreement do the bookkeeping.

label: Diffeomorphisms
notes: A diffeomorphism is the smooth notion of sameness: a smooth bijection with smooth inverse. The radial map sending the open ball onto all of Euclidean space is the standard example; radii near one are flung to infinity, which is why the boundary cannot belong to the domain. Diffeomorphic manifolds share dimension and every smooth invariant.

label: The Algebra C-infinity(M)
notes: Collect all smooth real-valued functions into one object. Pointwise sum and product make it a commutative algebra over the reals, with the constants sitting inside. Much of manifold theory is encoded here: later we recover tangent vectors as derivations of this algebra, so it pays to treat C-infinity of M as a first-class structure now.

label: Bump and Cutoff Functions
notes: Here is the analytic miracle that makes everything global possible. A function can be flat at a point, every derivative vanishing, yet positive nearby. From that flat seed we build a cutoff that slides from one to zero, and from the cutoff a radial bump equal to one on a set and supported in a slightly larger ball. No analytic function can do this.

label: Partitions of Unity
notes: State the theorem and the recipe. Given an open cover, there is a locally finite family of smooth weights, each supported in one cover set, all between zero and one, summing to one. The construction is mechanical: bumps inside refined coordinate balls, add them, local finiteness keeps the sum smooth and positive, then divide to normalize.

label: Proof Dependencies
notes: Make the logical scaffolding explicit so the proof stops feeling like a trick. Paracompactness supplies a locally finite refinement; regular coordinate balls supply room for bump supports; local finiteness makes the sum smooth; positivity of the total makes division legal; reindexing returns us to the original cover. Each link is necessary and the order matters.

label: Extension and Local-to-Global
notes: Close with the payoff. Gluing is rigid, used when local maps already agree on overlaps; blending is flexible, using partition weights when the codomain supports averages. The extension lemma then guarantees any smooth function on a closed set extends smoothly to the whole manifold, vanishing outside a chosen neighborhood. Local data becomes global geometry.
